AR.name: Urucu
AR.citation: Masa Americana regional-name survey. From Tupi-Guarani uruku, widely borrowed across South American languages for this species

BO.name: Urucu
BO.citation: Masa Americana regional-name survey; Salvia Paradise lists Bolivia among the largest annatto producers

BR.name: Urucum
BR.citation: Masa Americana; core of the species' native/production range (Grokipedia: Latin America ~60% of global annatto output, primarily Brazil and Peru). Also documented as acafrao, acafroa

CO.name: Achiote
CO.citation: Atlas de Plantas Medicinales, Norte del Cauca - comunidades afronortecaucanas (DHANA participatory research project)

CU.name: Bija
CU.citation: Masa Americana regional-name survey, shared with Peru

GT.name: Achiote
GT.citation: IPlantz; widely documented culinary use in Guatemala for coloring meat, fish and rice dishes when infused into cooking oil

IN.name: Sindhuri
IN.citation: IPlantz regional-name reference; also documented as Lathwa, Latkana. India is a genuine cultivation/production country for annatto, introduced under Spanish/Portuguese colonial trade

MX.name: Achiote
MX.citation: Masa Americana; Yogi's Gift. Name derives from Nahuatl achiotl; sacred to Maya and Aztec cultures as a symbolic blood substitute, used in Yucatecan cuisine (cochinita pibil) and Maya codex ink

PE.name: Bija
PE.citation: Masa Americana; Peru is among the largest global annatto producers/exporters (Yogi's Gift, Grokipedia)

PH.name: Achuete
PH.citation: IPlantz. Introduced to the Philippines in the 17th century by Spanish colonials from Central America/West Indies; now a major global production center

VE.name: Onoto
VE.citation: Melendez, Alvarado & Castro de Rojas (2012), market survey of medicinal plants sold in Maracay, Aragua, Venezuela. Also documented as onotillo
